Renaissance music, spanning roughly 1400 to 1600, is the transitional period between medieval and Baroque music, marked by the rise of polyphonic complexity, the dominance of human expression over liturgical constraint, and the gradual shift from sacred to secular interests. Centered in Italy and the Netherlandic composers who served Italian courts, Renaissance music bridged the medieval motet tradition and the Baroque innovations in harmony, tonality, and dramatic expression.

The Renaissance in music began earlier than in other arts, around 1400, with Franco-Flemish composers from modern Belgium and the Netherlands who introduced greater rhythmic regularity and harmonic sophistication. Polyphonic complexity reached new heights; composers like Josquin des Prez wrote motets and masses with five to six independent voice-parts woven in intricate counterpoint, yet with remarkable clarity and emotional impact. The rise of the madrigal in Italy reflected a Renaissance shift toward secular, vernacular art. Composers set Italian sonnets and lyric poetry with word-painting and emotional expression.

Printing and the spread of musical notation enabled composers to circulate works across Europe. Ottaviano Petrucci's invention of music printing in 1501 democratized the distribution of scores. Italy emerged as the musical center of Europe; Italian courts in Florence, Venice, Rome, and Naples became magnets for the greatest composers and fostered the development of new forms like opera and instrumental music. The Reformation in the early fifteen-hundreds led to the use of vernacular language and simpler musical styles in Protestant churches, contrasting with the Catholic Church's continued patronage of complex polyphony.

By the late Renaissance, in the fifteen-fifties through sixteen-hundreds, composers like Claudio Monteverdi were experimenting with harmonic boldness and new emotional intensity, prefiguring the Baroque style. Other major Renaissance composers include Josquin des Prez, who defined Renaissance polyphonic ideals; Orlando di Lasso, the prolific Franco-Flemish composer and bridge between Renaissance and early Baroque; and Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina, the exemplar of Renaissance mass and motet composition. The compositional techniques and spiritual depth achieved in the Renaissance—particularly polyphony, counterpoint, and the motet and madrigal forms—remain central to Western musical understanding.
